content: Acne Vulgaris Acne vulgaris is a common skin condition. In its earliest form, it presents without inflammation. The preferred treatment involves the application of Tretinoin cream (0.025% or 0.05%) or gel (0.01% or 0.025%) once daily. Alternatives include Adapalene 0.1% gel, Azelaic acid 20% cream, or Tazarotene 0.1% cream, all applied once daily. A reduction in comedones by 40–70% can be expected within 12 weeks. For mild inflammatory acne, the preferred regimen is a combination of Erythromycin 3% topical and Benzoyl peroxide 5% topical, applied twice daily. Alternatively, Clindamycin 1% gel and Benzoyl peroxide 5% topical can be used twice daily. Moderate to severe inflammatory acne may require Erythromycin 3% topical and Benzoyl peroxide 5% twice daily, with or without an oral antibiotic. Severe widespread nodular cystic lesions unresponsive to oral antibiotics may benefit from Isotretinoin (0.1–1 mg/kg) taken orally daily for 4–5 months. Alternative oral antibiotics include Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily or Minocycline 50 mg twice daily (or 1 mg/kg extended-release once daily). Other options include tetracycline, erythromycin, TMP-SMX, or clindamycin. Acne Rosacea For facial erythema associated with acne rosacea, Brimonidine gel is applied topically twice daily to the affected area. For papulopustular rosacea, the preferred treatments are Azelaic acid gel applied twice daily or Metronidazole cream applied once daily. Cutaneous Anthrax Cutaneous anthrax is treated with Penicillin V 500 mg orally four times daily for 7–10 days. Bacillary Angiomatosis Bacillary angiomatosis is treated with Erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily or Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 2 weeks to 2 months. In immunocompromised patients with relapse, retreatment may be required for 4–6 months, and repeated relapses may necessitate indefinite treatment. Long-term suppression with doxycycline or a macrolide is recommended for HIV-infected patients with a CD4 count <200 cells/mm³. Bite Wounds Animal Bites: The preferred treatment is Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily. Other options include Ampicillin-sulbactam intravenously, Piperacillin-tazobactam intravenously, Doxycycline orally or intravenously, or combinations such as Penicillin with Dicloxacillin. Additional alternatives include TMP-SMX, Metronidazole, Clindamycin, Cefuroxime, Cefoxitin, Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime, Ciprofloxacin, Levofloxacin, or Moxifloxacin. Human Bites: The preferred treatment is Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily. Alternatives include Ampicillin-sulbactam intravenously or Doxycycline orally. Lyme Disease Adults: Lyme disease is treated with Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily, Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily, or Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg orally twice daily. Severe cases may require Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously once daily. Alternatives include a single dose of Doxycycline 200 mg orally, Cefotaxime 2 g intravenously every 8 hours, or Penicillin G 18–24 million units/day intravenously. Pediatrics: Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day orally in three divided doses is preferred. For children aged ≥8 years, Doxycycline 4 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses is used. Cefuroxime axetil or Ceftriaxone may also be used. Alternatives include Doxycycline (for children <8 years), Cefotaxime, or Penicillin G. Bubonic Plague The preferred treatment for bubonic plague is Streptomycin 15 mg/kg intramuscularly every 12 hours. Alternatives include Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily or Gentamicin as a substitute for Streptomycin. Carbuncle Mild Cases: Incision and drainage are sufficient. Moderate Cases: Empiric treatment includes TMP-SMX or Doxycycline. MSSA infections are treated with TMP-SMX, while MRSA infections are treated with Dicloxacillin or Cephalexin. Severe Cases: Empiric treatment includes Vancomycin, Daptomycin, Linezolid, Televancin, or Ceftaroline. MSSA infections are treated with Nafcillin, Cefazolin, or Clindamycin, while MRSA infections are treated with Vancomycin, Daptomycin, Linezolid, Televancin, or Ceftaroline. Cat Scratch Disease For patients weighing >45 kg, Azithromycin 500 mg orally on day 1 followed by 250 mg daily for 4 additional days is recommended. For patients weighing <45 kg, Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally on day 1 followed by 5 mg/kg daily for 4 additional days is used. Cellulitis Non-purulent Cellulitis: Mild cases are treated with Penicillin VK, Cephalosporin, Dicloxacillin, or Clindamycin. Moderate cases may require intravenous Penicillin VK, Ceftriaxone, Cefazolin, or Clindamycin. Severe cases are treated with Vancomycin and Piperacillin-tazobactam. Purulent Cellulitis: Mild cases require incision and drainage. Moderate cases are treated with TMP-SMX or Doxycycline. Severe cases are treated with Vancomycin, Daptomycin, Linezolid, Televancin, or Ceftaroline. Ecthyma MSSA infections are treated with Dicloxacillin or Cephalexin. MRSA infections are treated with Doxycycline, Clindamycin, or TMP-SMX. Erysipelas Adults are treated with Penicillin, Amoxicillin, Erythromycin, Ceftriaxone, or Cefazolin. Pediatric cases are treated with Penicillin, Amoxicillin, Erythromycin, Ceftriaxone, or Cefazolin. Erysipeloid The preferred treatment is Penicillin 500 mg four times daily or Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7–10 days. Erythrasma Localized infections are treated with topical Clindamycin. Widespread infections are treated with Clarithromycin or Erythromycin orally for 14 days. Fournier Gangrene Streptococcal or clostridial infections are treated with Penicillin G. Polymicrobial infections are treated with Doripenem, Imipenem, or Meropenem. If MRSA is suspected, Vancomycin or Daptomycin is used. Furuncle Mild Cases: Incision and drainage are sufficient. Moderate Cases: Empiric treatment includes TMP-SMX or Doxycycline. MSSA infections are treated with TMP-SMX, while MRSA infections are treated with Dicloxacillin or Cephalexin. Severe Cases: Empiric treatment includes Vancomycin, Daptomycin, Linezolid, Televancin, or Ceftaroline. MSSA infections are treated with Nafcillin, Cefazolin, or Clindamycin, while MRSA infections are treated with Vancomycin, Daptomycin, Linezolid, Televancin, or Ceftaroline. Gas Gangrene Empiric therapy includes Vancomycin combined with Piperacillin-tazobactam, Ampicillin-sulbactam, or a carbapenem. For Clostridium perfringens, Penicillin G and Clindamycin are preferred. Glanders Treatment options include Ceftazidime, Gentamicin, Imipenem, Doxycycline, or Ciprofloxacin based on susceptibility. Mastitis Preferred treatments include Amoxicillin-clavulanate, Cephalexin, Ciprofloxacin, Clindamycin, Dicloxacillin, or TMP-SMX. Necrotizing Fasciitis Mixed infections are treated with Piperacillin-tazobactam and Vancomycin or carbapenems. Streptococcal infections are treated with Penicillin and Clindamycin. Staphylococcal infections are treated with Nafcillin, Oxacillin, Cefazolin, or Vancomycin. Clostridial infections are treated with Clindamycin and Penicillin. Pilonidal Cyst After pathogen identification, a 5–10 day course of antibiotics is prescribed. Pyomyositis Preferred treatments include Nafcillin, Oxacillin, or Cefazolin for MSSA. Vancomycin is used for MRSA. Seborrheic Dermatitis Antifungal agents such as Ketoconazole, Bifonazole, or Ciclopirox are used. Corticosteroids like Hydrocortisone, Betamethasone, or Clobetasol may also be applied. Lithium salts are another option. Skin and Soft Tissue Infections in Neutropenic Fever Initial treatment includes Vancomycin with a carbapenem or Piperacillin-tazobactam. Persistent cases may require antifungal therapy with agents like Fluconazole, Voriconazole, or Amphotericin-B. Surgical Site Infections Intestinal or genitourinary surgeries are treated with Ticarcillin-clavulanate, Piperacillin-tazobactam, or carbapenems. Trunk or extremity surgeries are treated with Oxacillin, Cefazolin, or Vancomycin. Tularemia Streptomycin or Gentamicin is preferred. Mild cases may be treated with Tetracycline or Doxycycline. Ulcerated Skin with Secondary Infection Treatment includes carbapenems, Ticarcillin-clavulanate, or Piperacillin-tazobactam. Alternatives include Ciprofloxacin or Levofloxacin with Metronidazole. Vibrio Infection Vibrio vulnificus infections are treated with Doxycycline and Ceftriaxone or Cefotaxime. Wound Infection Mild to moderate infections are treated with TMP-SMX or Clindamycin. Severe cases with sepsis require Ticarcillin-clavulanate or Piperacillin-tazobactam with Vancomycin. Yaws Treatment options include Phenoxymethylpenicillin, Tetracyclines, Erythromycin, or Azithromycin.
